cards.back: $v = \dfrac{d}{t}$, where $v$ = velocity (m/s or km/s), $d$ = distance (m or km), $t$ = time (s). Solved for the others: $d = vt$ and $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$.
How far something moves each unit of time: $\text{velocity} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. Same distance in half the time means twice the velocity.
A distance, not a time: how far a light wave travels in one year going at $c$. 100,000 ly means how far light would travel in 100,000 years.
$d = ct$, where $d$ = distance (m), $c = 3\times10^{8}$ m/s (the speed of light), $t$ = light-travel time (s). It is $v = \dfrac{d}{t}$ solved for $d$, with $c$ for the velocity.

cards.front: Work an example: how many meters is 1 light-year?
Work an example: how long does sunlight take to reach Earth (1 AU)?
cards.back: $t = \dfrac{d}{c} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}\ \text{m}}{3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}} = 500$ s $\approx 8.3$ min. We see the Sun as it was 8.3 minutes ago.

cards.front: Work an example: shrink the Sun (radius 696,340 km) to a 14 cm basketball. What is the shrink, and Earth's Scaled Dist.?
cards.back: Shrink $= \dfrac{6.96\times10^{10}\ \text{cm}}{14\ \text{cm}} \approx 5\times10^{9}$: a 5 billion times shrinking. Scaled Dist. $= \dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}\ \text{m}}{5\times10^{9}} = 30$ m. Same shrink for every size and distance; same units before you divide.

questions.stem: What is the speed of light in meters per second?
questions.explain: $c = 3\times10^{8}$ m/s. The $3\times10^{5}$ is the same speed in km/s, not m/s.

questions.stem: A light-year is a unit of…
questions.explain: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year going at $c$.

questions.stem: One light-year is about how many meters?
questions.explain: $1\ \text{ly} = 9.46\times10^{15}$ m. $1.5\times10^{11}$ m is 1 AU, and $6.31\times10^{4}$ is the number of AU in a light-year.
$v = \dfrac{d}{t}$: velocity is distance divided by time. Solved for distance it becomes $d = vt$.

questions.stem: Put these lengths in order, smallest first.
A planet orbits {d} AU from the Sun. How many minutes does sunlight take to reach it? (1 AU $= 1.5\times10^{11}$ m)
questions.explain: $t = \dfrac{ d }{c} = \dfrac{({d})(1.5\times10^{11}\ \text{m})}{3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}}$, then divide the seconds by 60: $t \approx$ {answer} min. (That is 8.3 min for every AU.)

questions.stem: A laser pulse is fired from Earth at a mirror the Apollo astronauts left on the Moon. The echo comes back {t} s after the pulse left. How far away is the Moon, in meters?
questions.explain: $d = ct$ gives the whole round trip, there and back. $d_{\rm round} = (3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s})({t}\ \text{s})$, and the Moon is half of that: {answer} m.

questions.stem: Voyager 1 is about {d} billion km from Earth. How many hours does a radio command, moving at $c$, take to reach it?
questions.explain: $t = \dfrac{ d }{v} = \dfrac{{d}\times10^{12}\ \text{m}}{3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}}$ in seconds, then divide by 3600 s/hr: $t \approx$ {answer} hr. A question and its answer take about two days round trip.

questions.stem: A star is {L} ly away. How far is that in meters?
A star is {d} trillion km away (1 trillion km $= 10^{15}$ m). How many light-years is that?
questions.explain: $d = \dfrac{{d}\times10^{15}\ \text{m}}{9.46\times10^{15}\ \text{m/ly}} =$ {answer} ly. Roughly 10 trillion km per light-year.

questions.stem: You shrink the Sun (radius 696,340 km) down to a beach ball of radius {r} cm. This represents a shrinking of how many times?
questions.explain: Put both radii in cm first: $696{,}340\ \text{km} = 6.96\times10^{10}$ cm. Shrink $= \dfrac{6.96\times10^{10}\ \text{cm}}{{r}\ \text{cm}} =$ {answer} times.

questions.stem: A scale model uses a {s} billion times shrinking. A planet orbits {d} AU from the Sun. What is its Scaled Dist., in meters? (1 AU $= 1.5\times10^{11}$ m)
Order of magnitude: in the basketball model (a 5 billion times shrinking), how far from the ball would Proxima Centauri (4.3 ly) sit? Pick the power of ten, in meters.
questions.explain: $\text{Scaled Dist.} = \dfrac{(4.3)(9.46\times10^{15}\ \text{m})}{5\times10^{9}} \approx 8\times10^{6}$ m, about 8,000 km. The planets fit in a walk through the Park Blocks; the nearest star does not fit on this continent.

questions.stem: Why do we see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago?
choices: The Sun's light is bent by Earth's air, which delays it
Our eyes and brain take about 8 minutes to process the image
The Sun only gives off light in bursts every 8 minutes
Its light needs about 8.3 minutes to cross the 1 AU to Earth
questions.explain: $t = \dfrac{d}{c} = \dfrac{1.5\times10^{11}\ \text{m}}{3\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s}} = 500$ s $\approx 8.3$ min. Light is fast, but not instant.

questions.stem: Alien astronomers (and a few of our own machines) look back at Earth. Because of light-travel time, each sees Earth at some time in the past. Order them from the most recent view of Earth to the oldest.
items: An alien in the Andromeda Galaxy
questions.explain: Farther away means the light left Earth longer ago. Moon: about a second. Mars: minutes. Neptune: hours. Proxima: 4.3 years. Andromeda: 2.2 million years, before there were humans.

questions.stem: A star 300 ly away explodes. On the star's own clock, the explosion happens tonight. When could astronomers on Earth first see it?
questions.explain: A distance of 300 ly means light needs 300 years to cross it. The light from tonight's explosion reaches Earth in 300 years. Turn it around: whatever we see from that star tonight left it 300 years ago.
